---
title: "Deviance residuals"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

After fitting a model, we need to ask where it fits poorly. For one binary row, the raw residual is $y_i-\widehat\pi_i$: the observed zero or one minus the fitted probability. When the observed response is one, this residual grows as the fitted probability moves away from one; when the response is zero, it grows in the opposite direction as the fitted probability moves away from zero.

Raw differences do not yet tell us how surprising those outcomes are under the fitted Bernoulli distribution. [**Deviance residuals**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) start from each row's loss in log likelihood relative to a perfect prediction. They take the square root of that loss and restore the sign of the raw residual. Squaring and adding them therefore recovers the model deviance.

Why not use only the raw difference $y_i-\widehat\pi_i$? A Bernoulli row has asymmetric available movement near zero and one. The deviance contribution derived from likelihood places that discrepancy on a common scale. Recall that a [residual](residuals.qmd) is observed minus fitted response, [standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd) is the square root of variance, and the likelihood product invokes [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd). The [expected value](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) of $Y_i$ is its fitted probability under the model.

We derive the signed contribution for one binary row, then aggregate the SuperTelicity pattern by verb while preserving the distinction between display summaries and sampling units.

$$
r_i^{D}=\operatorname{sign}(y_i-\widehat\pi_i)
\sqrt{2\left[y_i\log\frac{y_i}{\widehat\pi_i}+
(1-y_i)\log\frac{1-y_i}{1-\widehat\pi_i}\right]},
$$

with zero-times-log-zero terms defined as zero. We compute these residuals from the SuperTelicity interaction fit.

Recall that [deviance](deviance.qmd) is twice the log likelihood gap from the saturated fit. For one Bernoulli row, substitution gives two simple cases:

$$
d_i=
\begin{cases}
2\log(1/\widehat\pi_i), & y_i=1,\\
2\log[1/(1-\widehat\pi_i)], & y_i=0.
\end{cases}
$$

The residual is $\operatorname{sign}(y_i-\widehat\pi_i)\sqrt{d_i}$. The sign restores whether the observed value lies above or below its fitted mean; the square root makes squared residuals add to deviance.

```{r}
#| label: fit-deviance-residuals
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
st$contentfulness <- factor(st$contentfulness,
                            levels = c("contentful", "bleached", "templatic"))
fit <- glm(prep_in ~ verb_type * contentfulness, binomial(), st)
st$fitted <- fitted(fit)
st$deviance_residual <- residuals(fit, type = "deviance")
c(sum_squared = sum(st$deviance_residual^2), model_deviance = deviance(fit),
  minimum = min(st$deviance_residual), maximum = max(st$deviance_residual))
```

```{r}
#| label: one-deviance-residual-by-hand
#| echo: true
i <- 1L
manual_d <- if (st$prep_in[i] == 1) {
  2 * log(1 / st$fitted[i])
} else {
  2 * log(1 / (1 - st$fitted[i]))
}
data.frame(y = st$prep_in[i], fitted = st$fitted[i],
  raw = st$prep_in[i] - st$fitted[i],
  pearson = (st$prep_in[i] - st$fitted[i]) /
    sqrt(st$fitted[i] * (1 - st$fitted[i])),
  deviance_manual = sign(st$prep_in[i] - st$fitted[i]) * sqrt(manual_d),
  deviance_R = st$deviance_residual[i])
```

Raw residuals measure differences on the response scale. Pearson residuals divide that difference by the Bernoulli standard deviation. Deviance residuals instead encode a signed likelihood loss. These quantities answer different questions and need not rank rows identically.

The squared residuals sum to the model deviance. Binary row residuals are necessarily discrete-looking because each row contains only zero or one. We aggregate by verb only to display calibration; the fitted likelihood continues to use the individual rows.

```{r}
#| label: verb-calibration
#| echo: true
by_verb <- aggregate(cbind(prep_in, fitted) ~ verb, st, mean)
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(by_verb, aes(fitted, prep_in)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey65", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6, color = "#1F5A85") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Fitted in probability", y = "Observed in proportion by verb") +
  theme_classic()
```

Large gaps identify verbs for inspection, not automatically erroneous observations. They may indicate omitted lexical structure, dependence, or a mean specification that is too coarse. Because verbs, sentences, and participants recur, residual patterns should motivate a richer model rather than deletion based on a fixed threshold.

The verb proportions summarize the display. Their uncertainty depends on the number of trials and the repeated participant and sentence structure, so we cannot treat the points as new independent observations or interpret distance from the diagonal as a calibrated test.

## Recap and check

1. Why can binary row residuals not form a smooth cloud around zero? Each observed row is only zero or one.
2. Does a large deviance residual prove a bad data point? No. It marks a large fitted likelihood loss and can instead reveal omitted structure or dependence.

We apply related diagnostics to [Poisson regression](poisson-regression.qmd), where row outcomes have more than two possible values.
